# @codenhub/oidc/testing

## Functions

### createMemoryStore

```ts
export declare function createMemoryStore(options?: MemoryStoreOptions): MemoryStore;
```

Creates an in-memory [MemoryStore](#memorystore) that keeps everything in one process's memory.

Everything lives in this process's memory and is lost on restart. It is NOT for production: it exists for tests and examples, and it is the reference for the [OidcStore](provider.md#oidcstore) contract that other adapters are judged against.

Records are never purged. The store keeps every record for its lifetime, and the provider checks `expiresAt` itself, so memory grows with use; that is one more reason it is not for production. Saved and returned records are copies, so the caller can change its own objects without changing the store.

**Parameters**

- `options` — Clients to register.

**Returns** — A store whose methods resolve for any string key, except that each `save*` method rejects when its key already exists, so a spent code or refresh token can never be made consumable again.

### StoreConformanceCase

```ts

```

One check of the OidcStore contract. `run` resolves when the store conforms and rejects with an Error naming the broken rule otherwise.

### StoreSeed

```ts
export interface StoreSeed
```

What a case asks the store under test to hold before it runs. The `OidcStore` interface has no method that saves a client, so the factory registers these clients itself, the way the app's admin side would.

#### clients

```ts
readonly clients: readonly ClientRecord[];
```

Clients `findClient` must return. Their identifiers are random per case.

## Variables

### storeConformanceCases

```ts
export declare const storeConformanceCases: readonly StoreConformanceCase[];
```

Every check of the OidcStore contract, for any test runner: `for (const c of storeConformanceCases) it(c.name, () => c.run((seed) => createStore(seed)))`.

Each case calls `createStore(seed)` once and runs against the store it returns, which must hold the clients in `seed.clients` and nothing else the case relies on. Most cases pass no clients. Keys, grant identifiers and client identifiers are random per case, so cases never collide even when they share one database. Failures are plain `Error`s whose message names the broken rule and never a key or token value.

Wire the suite into a runner by calling each case with a factory for the adapter under test. With Node.js's built-in runner:

**Example**

```ts
import { describe, test } from "node:test";
import { storeConformanceCases } from "@codenhub/oidc/testing";

describe("OidcStore", () => {
  for (const c of storeConformanceCases) {
    test(c.name, () =>
      c.run(async ({ clients }) => {
        for (const client of clients) {
          await registerClient(env.DB, client); // the app's own admin write
        }
        return createD1Store(env.DB);
      }),
    );
  }
});
```

Vitest and Jest work the same way, with their `describe` and `it`.
